segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
The whole thing is glass. It stands about 28 centimetres tall. Two long tentacles hang from it, and seven shorter ones. You can count them. It rests on a green wire rod.

This is a Portuguese man o' war. In New Zealand waters it is better known as the bluebottle. Its other name comes from its resemblance to an 18th-century Portuguese sailing warship.

segments.heading: Not one animal
segments.text:
A man o' war is related to true jellyfish. But it is not one. And it is not a single creature either.

It is a colonial organism, made up of many individual organisms called zooids. Zooids stay connected as they grow. Each one has its own specialised job. None of them can survive alone.

segments.heading: A float, and a sail
segments.text:
Look at the top section. In a living man o' war that part does two jobs at once. It is a float, and it is a sail. They travel on the currents and the wind.

Every man o' war is either left-handed or right-handed, depending on which way that sail curves.

The tentacles below can reach ten metres. They catch small crustaceans and fish.

floating-colonies.panel: A Portuguese man o' war is not one animal. It is hundreds, fused into a single drifting colony — some members sting, some digest, some reproduce — and not one of them could survive alone. What you are looking at is less a creature than a crew.
floating-colonies.ending: These go where the water goes. The next page belongs to animals that solved the same problem — open water, nowhere to hide — a completely different way.
